cards.title: Market-First Product Research Hierarchy
cards.summary: Choose a passionate market and an emotional problem before picking a product, because market and problem drive sales more than the product itself.
cards.use_when: Starting a new ecommerce product search, or when a previous product test failed and you're tempted to jump straight to product hunting.
steps: Start with market research, not product research. The presenter argues the market influences success far beyond the product, using the analogy of selling umbrellas in a thunderstorm versus on a sunny day: same product, very different sales volume.

Pick from markets known for passion and emotion: pets, weight loss, hair growth, cosmetics/skincare (anything with a clear before-and-after transformation), supplements, beauty, health and wellness. The presenter says these markets are broad enough that the market itself won't be the reason for failure.
Narrow to an emotional problem inside that market before choosing the physical product. Examples given: lower back stiffness, neck and shoulder tension, plantar fasciitis, migraines.

Keep the problem broad enough to support many products. One winning problem (e.g. migraines) can be solved by supplements, a head band, a massage gun, a neck traction device, or a clinic visit — so you have many product options and room to test.
Only then select the actual product that solves the chosen problem.
Don't overthink market selection — pick one and move on. The presenter explicitly frames this as the easiest, most spoonfed part of the process.
caveats: 'Market first' is the presenter's opinion and framework, not a proven law; it does not remove the need for validation and a solid funnel.
The listed markets are his examples, not a guaranteed set — supplements in particular he calls challenging despite long-term potential.

cards.title: Use Claude to Generate Winning Emotional Sub-Niches
cards.summary: Prompt Claude (Opus or Sonnet) to produce a list of emotional sub-niches downstream from your chosen market, then pick five to research further.
cards.use_when: You have picked a market and want a fast list of specific emotional problems to build products and offers around.
steps: Open Claude directly — the presenter used Opus (he says Sonnet would likely be fine) and states no other tool (e.g. Fable) is needed for this step.
Paste a large structured prompt asking for a list of emotional sub-niches for a DTC beginner brand in your chosen market. The output shown in the video was a list of 30 sub-niches.

Review the list for problems with demonstrated commercial history — his examples: lower back stiffness, neck and shoulder tension, plantar fasciitis. He claims each of these has multiple seven- and eight-figure businesses inside it.
Select five sub-niches you like most. These five become the search scope you feed into the next step (ad-spy tool via MCP).
Treat the AI output as candidate problems, not validated winners — the validation step with real competitor traffic data comes later.
caveats: The exact models, prompt text and list quality decay quickly; verify what the current Claude interface and models actually produce.
The presenter's claim that each sub-niche contains multiple seven/eight-figure businesses is his assertion, not measured evidence.

cards.title: Connect Get Hooked to Claude via MCP for Ad-Library Sourcing
cards.summary: Wire the Get Hooked ad-aggregator MCP server into Claude as a custom connector so the AI can pull live competitor brand and ad data.
cards.use_when: You want Claude to research real competitor brands, active ads, angles and funnels instead of relying on its training data alone.
steps: Create an account (the presenter used a free trial) at get hooked.ai.
In Get Hooked, open your account menu (bottom-left), then select 'AI and MCP'.
Scroll past the API section to the 'Connect to AI agent' / MCP section.
Copy the MCP server URL and the OAuth Client ID shown there.
In Claude, go to the left-hand sidebar, select 'Customize', then 'Connectors', then the plus icon, then 'Add custom connector'.
Name it (e.g. 'Get Hooked'), paste the MCP server URL, then paste the OAuth Client ID into the corresponding field, and click Add.
You now effectively have Claude plus a large Facebook/Meta ad library in one interface. Verify the current menu labels and flow, since MCP connectors and UIs change quickly.
caveats: Exact UI paths and field names are high-decay — confirm them in both tools before relying on this sequence.
Get Hooked is described as a free trial; pricing and access may change.

cards.title: Run the MCP Product-Sourcing Prompt Over Your Five Sub-Niches
cards.summary: Feed the MCP-connected Claude a prompt with MCP usage instructions plus your five chosen sub-niches to return qualifying brands, pain points, ad patterns and funnels.
cards.use_when: Claude is connected to the Get Hooked MCP and you have narrowed to five emotional sub-niches.
steps: Write one prompt that includes (a) information about the MCP and how to use it, (b) the research process Claude should follow, and (c) the five sub-niches you selected earlier.
Submit and let it run — the presenter says this takes a few minutes.

Read the output: qualifying brands that are running enough active ads and fit your input sub-niches. For each, the output shown included the product, the pain point, the ad pattern typically used, the funnel architecture (e.g. driving to a PDP vs. an advertorial), and a top-performing ad.
Use the funnel-architecture field as competitive intelligence, not just the product name — it tells you where competitors send traffic.
The presenter's example find: a Facebook page 'Fall Prevention Tips' running 232 active ads across a few subdomains, selling wide toe box barefoot shoes with a foot-pain angle.
The presenter claims this makes product selection achievable in about an hour with the right tools.
caveats: The hour-long claim is the presenter's experience, not a benchmark.
Qualifying criteria come from active ad volume, which can reflect budget or testing rather than proven profitability — validate separately.
The exact prompt contents are not fully reproduced in the source; reconstruct to fit your own sub-niches.

cards.title: Estimate Competitor Revenue with the SimilarWeb Formula
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer a competitor's monthly revenue floor as monthly visits × estimated conversion rate × estimated AOV, and require roughly $200k–$300k+/month before treating them as proof of a winning product.
cards.use_when: Validating whether brands surfaced by your ad-spy research are actually selling at scale.
steps: Install the SimilarWeb extension and open the competitor's store page with it enabled to read estimated monthly visits. The presenter notes about three free searches per day.
Estimate a conversion rate. He uses a baseline of 2% and typically ranges 1.5%–3.5%; he says the more expensive the product, the lower the rate tends to be (e.g. ~1.5% for high-ticket).
Estimate an AOV conservatively, using the visible offer stack as a guide. In his example the store sold shoes at $70/pair and he estimated AOV around $90, using $90 as a conservative figure.
Multiply: monthly visits × conversion rate = monthly orders; then × estimated AOV = estimated monthly revenue.
Example from the video: 1.5 million visits (conservative, actual ~2M) × 2% = ~30,000 orders; × $90 AOV = ~$2.7M/month.
Set a floor: the presenter says he only wants to see candidates above roughly $200k–$300k/month in estimated revenue.
caveats: These are rough estimates, not financials — the presenter states plainly he cannot calculate exact revenue.
Both conversion rate and AOV are assumptions; conservative inputs make the floor more trustworthy than an optimistic guess.
SimilarWeb visit figures are estimates and free-tier search limits apply.

cards.title: The Two Golden Margin Rules: 3x COGS and $30 Gross Margin
cards.summary: Require at least 3x cost of goods sold at retail price and at least $30 of gross margin per unit so the product can absorb rising Meta ad costs.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a sourced product can support paid acquisition before committing to a test.
steps: Rule one: price at minimum 3x your landed cost of goods sold (sourced plus shipped). If it costs $15 landed, sell at $45 or more.
Rule two: keep at least $30 of gross profit per unit. The presenter says he used to use $20 and raised it because Facebook ad costs keep increasing.
Check both rules at once. Example: source for $15, sell for $50 gives a $35 gross margin — this satisfies both the 3x multiplier and the $30 floor.
Account for the fact that established competitors have negotiated better supplier rates than a new dropshipping brand, so do not assume you can match their cost base.
caveats: These are the presenter's rules of thumb for a specific ad-cost environment, not universal economics.
3x COGS with a $30 floor can conflict at low price points — a $12 product gives 3.6x but only ~$36 margin, while a $10 product at 3x yields only $20 margin and fails rule two.
Margins must also cover shipping, payment fees and refunds; the rules as stated only address ad costs.

cards.title: Diagnose a Failed Product Test: Ads Problem or Funnel Problem
cards.summary: After a failed test, ask 'why' and split the cause into ad-related issues (CPC/CTR/CPM) or funnel-related issues (ATC, checkout completion, AOV) before abandoning the product.
cards.use_when: A product test underperforms and you're deciding whether to kill the product, fix creatives, or fix the funnel.
steps: Run the full process — market, problem, product selection, validation, then a sales game plan — before concluding the method failed. The presenter stresses that people often test with no plan and quit at the first unprofitable day.
Recognize that the product is rarely the issue. The presenter says top six-, seven- and eight-figure brands sell nothing especially remarkable; they have ads and funnel dialed in.
Ask which bucket the failure falls into: ad-related (creatives not good enough) or funnel-related (store, advertorial or checkout not good enough).
If concrete funnel KPI checks surface a checkout or payment-processing problem, fix that before touching the product.
The presenter claims roughly 90% of the failures he sees are ad-related, usually because sellers believe their ads are good when they aren't.
caveats: The 90% figure is the presenter's observation, not a measured statistic.
This is in scope as test-triage, but optimizing the ads themselves belongs to creative and media-buying work, and fixing the checkout belongs to storefront work.

cards.title: Ad Failure KPIs: CPC, CTR and CPM Thresholds
cards.summary: Use link CPC above $1.50, CTR below 3%, and CPM above $80 as indicators that a failed test is an advertising problem, usually a creative problem.
cards.use_when: A US product test is unprofitable and you need to determine whether the ads, not the offer or product, are the constraint.
steps: Read link CPC first: target roughly $1.50 for US targeting. If it's elevated — $2, $3, $4 — treat it as a check-engine light: it signals something is wrong but not what.
Check CTR next: aim for a 3% minimum, and the presenter prefers closer to 4%. A sub-3% CTR means a serious creative problem — weak hooks or copy.
If CTR is healthy (4–5%) but CPC is still elevated, look at CPM. He offers no strict CPM KPI and calls it niche- and location-dependent, but says above roughly $80 CPM in the US is on the high end.
Note the feedback loop: poor creatives both lower CTR and raise CPM because the platform penalizes low-engagement ads, producing a high CPC.
Resist maxing CTR for vanity. High-CTR curiosity/native creatives that don't convert mean you forgot to sell — balance engagement with conversion intent.
caveats: Thresholds are US-specific and will decay as ad costs change; treat them as directional.
The presenter explicitly says CPM targets are relative and have no fixed KPI — the $80 line is his rough guide, not a rule.

cards.title: Funnel Failure KPIs: ATC Ratio, Checkout Completion and AOV
cards.summary: Use landing-page-to-add-to-cart below 10%, ATC-to-purchase below 30%, and AOV under a 20–40% markup over base price as indicators that the failed test is a funnel problem.
cards.use_when: Ad metrics look acceptable but the product still isn't converting, or you need to locate friction between click and purchase.
steps: Add-to-cart ratio: of everyone who lands on the first page (advertorial, pre-sell page, or PDP), at least 10% should add to cart. This is somewhat price-dependent — for more expensive products 8–9% can be acceptable. Below that, the funnel or the traffic quality is failing.

ATC-to-purchase ratio: aim for 30% completion, so 3 of every 10 add-to-carts purchase. Below 30% points to friction between cart and purchase — check payment-processor approval rates and simplify the checkout. The presenter favors removing steps over adding conversion bumpers.

AOV: on a straight Shopify setup, target AOV 20–40% above the base selling price (he suggests pushing even 50% above for a one-product store). A low AOV usually means missing upsells or downsells on the first purchase.
LTV: for subscription or retention-heavy models, LTV should be substantially higher than AOV. A low LTV means you acquire customers reasonably well but don't earn enough from them over time.
caveats: These are the presenter's working benchmarks, not validated universal thresholds; they vary with price point and model.
ATC and checkout figures can be distorted by bot traffic or by traffic quality from the ad itself, so read the ad and funnel metrics together.

cards.title: Keep AI Sourcing and Ad Execution in Separate Ownership
cards.summary: AI-assisted sourcing ends at a validated, margin-checked product; creative, media buying and storefront work are separate disciplines that determine whether the product actually succeeds.
cards.use_when: Scoping a product-research sprint, or setting expectations that finding the product is only one part of a profitable launch.
steps: Delimit the sourcing workflow to: market selection, emotional problem identification, product selection via AI plus ad-spy data, competitor revenue validation, margin checks, and a basic test-triage game plan.
Route creative writing and ad design to your creative process — the sourcing workflow does not produce winning ads.
Route bid management and CPC/CPM optimization to paid-media execution.
Route checkout-flow and landing-page layout changes to storefront work.
Treat the KPI thresholds in this method as validation and triage signals for a product test, not as a substitute for media-buying or funnel-building skills.
Use this split when briefing a team or reviewing a failed test, so you don't replace a creative or checkout fix with another product search.
caveats: The source maps these boundaries as a module taxonomy; it does not argue paid media or creative are unimportant — the reverse.

input.text:
Process and Classify Information:

Topic: Product Research using AI (Claude + Get Hooked MCP), Market Selection, Formula for estimating competitor revenue, Margin math, and Post-launch troubleshooting (Ads vs. Funnel KPIs).

Core Concepts:

Market First, Product Second: Pick a passionate market (pet, weight loss, hair growth, skincare, health). Identify the emotional problem first (e.g., lower back stiffness, plantar fasciitis).

Tool Setup: Claude + Get Hooked MCP (Model Context Protocol). Connects the AI to a Facebook Ads aggregator.

Competitor Validation (SimilarWeb Math): Est Revenue = (Monthly Visits) x (Estimated Conversion Rate ~2%) x (Estimated AOV). Benchmark is finding competitors making >$300k/mo.

Margin Rules: 3x Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). Minimum $30 gross margin to absorb Meta ad costs.

Post-Launch Troubleshooting (The "Why"):

Ads Issue: CPC target $1.50 (US). CTR target >3% (ideally 4%). High CPMs (> $80) indicate poor creative engagement.

Funnel Issue: Add-to-Cart (ATC) ratio >10%. ATC to Purchase ratio >30%. AOV target 20-40% above the base selling price.

Module fit: This blends Product Validation [02-PRD] with Performance Ad Execution [04-MED] (troubleshooting CPC/CTR) and Storefront Architecture [05-WEB] (ATC/Purchase ratios).

Decision: The core focus of the video is finding and validating the product using Claude + Get Hooked and SimilarWeb, culminating in the margin rules. The troubleshooting section is "what to do when the product fails," which bridges into adjacent modules. I will classify the primary extraction under [02-PRD] / AI-Assisted Product Sourcing and map the troubleshooting metrics strictly to the "Look for" section as validation KPIs for a product test, while explicitly bounding out the actual ad creation and funnel building to [03-CRE], [04-MED], and [05-WEB].

Header Details:

url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1KrsOagtWgM

source_date: 2026-06

verified_at: 2026-09-19

rights: public_reference

why: Connects Claude directly to the Get Hooked ad library via MCP for automated sourcing, and provides exact formulas to calculate competitor revenue and troubleshoot failed product tests.

modules: [[02-PRD]]

topics: [[AI Sourcing, Claude MCP, Margin Math, Revenue Estimation, Troubleshooting KPIs, Problem Identification]]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

decay_risk: high (Claude MCP integrations and exact ad costs decay rapidly).

Format into Taxonomy:

Scope definition: Workflows for using AI (Claude) connected to ad spy tools (Get Hooked) via MCP to source high-margin products solving emotional pain points. Includes mathematical formulas for estimating competitor revenue via SimilarWeb and KPI benchmarks for troubleshooting failed product tests.
